adopets.title: Adopets
adopets.sub: A platform for pet-store networks, from the database to the shared UI.

why.title: Why build it
why.p1: A pet store is more than a shop: it sells products, keeps stock, books the vet and remembers every animal. A chain multiplies that by every location, and each person should see only what their role and store allow.
why.p2: I wanted to practice monorepo boundaries, permission modeling and a shared UI package in a domain that feels real.

arch.title: Three apps, one source of truth.

boxes.label: apps/server
boxes.value: Fastify and Prisma REST API, JWT auth

access.title: Who sees what, and where.
access.body: Roles are checked in middleware: the store comes from the token, and a permission helper decides what each role can do on each resource.

items.title: A monorepo for one person
items.body: Shared types, UI and config between web and API keep the codebase consistent. Turborepo makes builds and tasks fast even solo.

items.title: Roles live on the store, not the user
items.body: A person can be ADMIN in one store and EMPLOYEE in another, so the join table is role × store × user. This matches the business better than a global role.

items.title: Validate at the edge
items.body: Zod validates every route input and the environment. Failures become type errors before runtime surprises.

items.title: Domain-shaped routes
items.body: Routes are grouped by domain — auth, user, product, transaction — instead of by technical layer, so the API reads like the product.

next.body: Add an audit log for sales, expose a live demo and raise test coverage for the permission layer. Showing the gaps is part of senior work.

adopets.quote: The hardest part was not the schema; it was deciding who gets to see which row.
